subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Port Royal: The Wickedest City on Earth
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Port Royal: The Wickedest City on Earth.

hook.text: Jamaica's pirate capital sank into the sea during an earthquake in 1692. The church bell still tolled underwater.

buildup.text: Port Royal was the richest and most notorious city in the Caribbean — a haven for pirates, rum, and vice.

discovery.text: Divers found a pocket watch stopped at 11:43 AM — the exact moment the earthquake struck on June 7, 1692.

twist.text: The city sat on loose sand. Liquefaction turned the ground to liquid, swallowing two-thirds of the town in minutes.

climax.text: Preachers called it divine punishment for sin. Survivors rebuilt — and the new city sank again in a 1907 earthquake.

punchline.text: God sank the pirate city. They rebuilt. It sank again.

quiz.question: What artifact helped pinpoint the exact time of Port Royal's earthquake?
options: A ship's log found in the harbor with the date and time
A pocket watch stopped at 11:43 AM on June 7, 1692
A church clock found still ticking underwater

details.summary: Port Royal, Jamaica, was once the wealthiest and most notorious pirate haven in the Caribbean until a massive earthquake in 1692 plunged two-thirds of the city into the sea.
details.whyItMatters: Port Royal is a time capsule of 17th-century colonial Caribbean life. Unlike most historical cities where continuous occupation destroys earlier layers, Port Royal was frozen in a single catastrophic moment and preserved underwater.
takeaways: A notorious pirate haven destroyed by an earthquake in 1692
Two-thirds of the city sank into the sea during the earthquake

faq.question: How much of Port Royal has been explored?
faq.answer: Only about five percent of the submerged city has been excavated. The remains lie in poor-visibility water with challenging conditions. faq.question: Why was Port Royal called the wickedest city on Earth?
faq.answer: English buccaneers used Port Royal as their base for raiding Spanish treasure ships. The city had more taverns per square foot than any other in the Caribbean. Enormous wealth from piracy funded a debauched lifestyle that horrified visiting clergy and delighted visiting sailors.
